title: Clinical, Immunological, Biochemical and Safety Outcomes of Eryxin (Reptilin) in Human Studies: A Systematic Review of Published and Grey Literature
content: Background. Eryxin (Reptilin), an aqueous snake autolysate developed in Uzbekistan, has been used since the 1990s as an immunomodulating agent. Its clinical evidence is dispersed across published and grey literature.Objective. To identify and appraise human studies of Eryxin or Reptilin and summarise their clinical, immunological, biochemical and safety outcomes.Methods. We searched PubMed, Europe PMC, Google Scholar, eLIBRARY.ru, CyberLeninka, three trial registries, libraries and archives; the last search update was on 30 September 2026. Human studies of any design with extractable data were eligible. Authors independently extracted data with artificial-intelligence assistance; discrepancies were checked against original scans. Two reviewer pairs independently assessed risk of bias for prioritised outcomes using the 2016 Risk Of Bias In Non-randomised Studies of Interventions tool for controlled studies and the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute before–after tool for uncontrolled studies. Synthesis was descriptive without meta-analysis. Certainty was summarised by condition and for adverse events using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach.Results. Twenty-two non-randomised studies across 16 conditions were included (64 reports), all conducted in Uzbekistan. A reliable total number of unique participants was unavailable because of uncertain cohort overlap and inconsistent participant counts. Most reports were retrieved from libraries and archives. Eleven of 16 controlled studies were at serious and five at critical risk of bias; all six uncontrolled studies were rated poor. Eryxin was added to other treatment in all but one arm. Favourable clinical and laboratory findings were reported, but interpretation was limited by confounding, incomplete reporting and, in some studies, differing co-interventions. Immunological findings varied across conditions and regimens without establishing a consistent response. Reporting gaps or inconsistencies were identified in 18 studies. Reported adverse events included transient taste or odour, flushing, tachycardia, fever and rash; ascertainment and denominators were inconsistent. Recorded certainty ratings were very low across conditions and for adverse events.Conclusions. The evidence does not establish effectiveness for any studied condition. This does not demonstrate absence of an effect. Overall and comparative safety remain uncertain. Well-conducted randomised controlled trials are needed to determine clinical benefits and harms.
